claims.source: This analysis highlighted a distinct clustering of lipid peaks representing cholesterol, triglycerides, and fatty acids (Feuerer et al., 2021) around LD-R amastigotes, contrasting with their minimal clustering around LD-S amastigotes which resemble uninfected-KCs more closely (Figure 3Ei).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3Ei and citation.

claims.claim: LDL uptake by LD-infected-KCs is independent of the host's LDL receptor.
claims.source: However, immunofluorescence analysis showed a decrease in LDLr expression in infected KCs harboring LD-amastigotes as compared to adjacent uninfected KCs, regardless of infection type (Figure 4A), along with no significant changes in total LDLr expression between uninfected, LD-S, and LD-R-infected-KCs, as observed from western blot (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). This indicated that LDL uptake by LD-infected-KCs might be receptor independent.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Infecting LDLr-KD-PEC with LD-S or LD-R resulted in no significant changes in intracellular amastigote numbers compared to scrambled RNA control.
claims.source: Infecting LDLr-KD-PEC with LD-S or LD-R resulted in no significant changes in intracellular amastigote numbers for both infection types as compared to scrambled RNA control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) confirming that although LD-R relies on increased LDL-influx for heightened proliferation, this influx is LDLr independent.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Western blot analysis revealed an increase in Cofilin levels with a concurrent decrease in its phosphorylated form as LD-R-infection progressed.
claims.source: Western blot analysis of infected KCs revealed an increase in Cofilin levels with a concurrent decrease in its phosphorylated form as LD-R-infection progressed, indicating active fluid-phase endocytosis (Figure 4Bi, ii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4Bi, ii.

claims.claim: Latrunculin-A treatment prevented the uptake of fluorescent red-LDL and severely impacted intracellular proliferation of LD-R amastigotes.
claims.source: Real-time fluorescence tracking demonstrated that Latrunculin-A treatment not only prevented the uptake of fluorescent red-LDL but also severely impacted intracellular proliferation of LD-R amastigotes (Video 3A, B and Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Video 3A, B and Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Treatment with Cytochalasin-D had no effect on the intracellular proliferation of LD-R.
claims.source: In contrast, treatment with Cytochalasin-D, which alters cellular F-actin organization but does not affect fluid-phase endocytosis (Lucero et al., 2020), had no effect on the intracellular proliferation of LD-R irrespective of Cytochalasin-D concentrations (2.5 and 5 µg/ml, respectively) (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, and citation.

claims.claim: An increased convergence of LDL-vesicles with LAMP-1-positive LD-R-PV was observed at 4 hr post-infection.
claims.source: LD-PV are modified phagolysosomes (Pessoa et al., 2019; Verma et al., 2017), and we observed an increased convergence of LDL-vesicles with LAMP-1-positive LD-R-PV even at 4 hr p.i., while such convergence was not noticed in LD-S-infected-KC (Figure 5Ai, ii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5Ai, ii and citations.

claims.claim: Structured illumination microscopy confirmed a complete convergence of LDL-vesicles with LD-R-PV at 24 hr post-infection.
claims.source: Structured illumination microscopy confirmed a complete convergence of LDL-vesicles with LD-R-PV at 24 hr p.i., while LD-S-PV showed only partial convergence with LDL-vesicles even at this late infection point (Figure 5Bi, ii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5Bi, ii.

claims.claim: Filipin staining revealed enhanced cholesterol accumulation surrounding LD-R amastigotes compared to LD-S amastigotes.
claims.source: Filipin staining of EGFP-LD-S and EGFP-LD-R-infected KCs at 24 hr p.i. revealed enhanced cholesterol accumulation surrounding LD-R amastigotes, as indicated by a significantly higher co-localization coefficient compared to LD-S amastigotes (Figure 5Di–iii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5Di–iii.

claims.claim: RNAseq analysis showed suppressed expression of Npc1 in LD-R-infected-MΦs.
claims.source: Analysis of available RNAseq (INRP000146) data for uninfected, LD-S and LD-R-infected-PEC (Figure 6A) revealed a suppression of Npc1 expression along with its transcription factor Srebp2 (Garver et al., 2008), in response to LD-R-infection.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6A and citation.

claims.claim: Western blot analysis confirmed low expression of SREBP2 and NPC-1 in LD-R-infected-KC at 24 hr post-infection.
claims.source: Western blot analysis of LD-S and LD-R-infected-KCs confirmed this low expression of SREBP2 and NPC-1 in LD-R-infected-KC 24 hr p.i. (Figure 6Bi, ii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6Bi, ii.

claims.claim: SREBP2 showed minimal nuclear translocation in LD-R-infected macrophages compared to LD-S-infected cells.
claims.source: More interestingly, confocal imaging not only confirmed this low expression of SREBP2, but even in those cases of LD-R-infected-KCs where we did observe some residual expression of SREBP2, it was entirely restricted to cytoplasm, unlike LD-S or uninfected-KCs where SREBP2 did get translocated in the nucleus (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: siRNA-mediated KD of NPC-1 in PEC resulted in significant increase in amastigote load in response to LD-R-infection.
claims.source: Finally, siRNA-mediated KD of NPC-1 in PEC (due to failure of successful KD generation in KCs), resulted in significant increase in amastigote load in response to LD-R-infection, while no such change in amastigote load was observed for LD-S-infected NPC-1-KD-PECs (Figure 6Gi–iv).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6Gi–iv.

claims.claim: LD-R-infected-KCs showed low IFN-γ levels even after 24 hr of co-culture with T-cells.
claims.source: Surprisingly, our ELISA results showed a low IFN-γ levels in the culture supernatant of LD-R-infected-KCs even after 24 hr of co-culture, while for LD-S-infection a significant increase was noted at this point (Figure 7Bi).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7Bi.

claims.claim: LD-S or LD-R-infected-KCs incubated with ox-LDL showed significant purple positive staining of ox-LDL only for LD-S-infected-KCs.
claims.source: LD-S or LD-R-infected-KCs incubated with ox-LDL showed a significant purple positive staining of ox-LDL only for LD-S-infected-KCs (Figure 7Ci), with LD-R-infected-KCs seemingly inhibiting uptake of ox-LDL.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7Ci.

claims.claim: Confocal images and western blot analysis confirmed a significant lower expression of MSR-1 in LD-R-infected-KCs compared to LD-S-infected-KCs.
claims.source: Confocal images and western blot analysis confirmed a significant lower expression of MSR-1 in LD-R-infected-KCs as compared to LD-S-infected-KCs (Figure 7Di, ii), thus explaining reduced staining for ox-LDL in response to LD-R-infection.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7Di, ii.

claims.claim: Immunostaining of liver sections from 28 days LD-R-infected mice confirmed significantly lower expression of MSR-1 with higher accumulation of neutral lipid droplets compared to LD-S-infected murine liver.
claims.source: Finally, immunostaining of liver sections from 28 days LD-S and LD-R-infected mice (Figure 7Fi) confirmed a significant lower expression of MSR-1 in LD-R-infected liver with higher accumulation of neutral lipid droplets as compared to LD-S-infected murine liver (Figure 7Fii, iii), thus confirming LD-R specifically accumulates neutral lipids by restricting MSR-1 expression.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7Fi, Fii, Fiii.

claims.claim: Lipid droplets staining revealed significantly higher lipid droplets accumulation around LD-R amastigotes.
claims.source: Lipid droplets staining of LD-S and LD-R-infected-KCs revealed significantly higher lipid droplets accumulation around LD-R amastigotes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and Video 4.

claims.claim: TEM showed lipid droplets accumulating around LD-R amastigotes.
claims.source: This was further confirmed by performing transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in LD-R-infected-KC which showed lipid droplets accumulating around LD-R amastigotes (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Two LD-R-strains (BHU575 and BHU814) showed reduced responsiveness against Amp-B with EC50 of 0.39 and 0.31 μM respectively, compared to EC50 of 0.03 μM for LD-S1 and 0.032 μM LD-S2.
claims.source: Interestingly, we noted that two LD-R-strains (BHU575 and BHU814) which we have included in this study also shows reduced responsiveness against Amp-B, a second-line-antileishmanial (Ghosh et al., 2021), and we validate this by determining their EC50 against Amp-B in LD-infected-KCs, which showed an EC50 of 0.39 and 0.31 μM for LD-R1 and LD-R2 amastigotes, respectively, as compared to EC50 of 0.03 μM for LD-S1 and 0.032 μM LD-S2.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding stated in the text and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Low lipid medium resulted in enhanced susceptibility for both LD-R strains against Amp-B with EC50 reduced to 0.39–0.16 μM for LD-R1 and 0.31–0.06 μM for LD-R2.
claims.source: Low lipid medium results in significant drop in lipid droplets accumulation within LD-R-infected-KCs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) and also resulted in enhanced susceptibility for both the LD-R strains against Amp-B with EC50 reduced to 0.39–0.16 μM for LD-R1 and 0.31–0.06 μM for LD-R2 as compared to high lipid medium (Figure 8Ci, ii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and Figure 8Ci, ii.

claims.claim: Lab-generated Amphotericin-B-unresponsive LD promastigotes (LD-SAmp-B-R) did not result in significant lipid droplets accumulation around amastigotes.
claims.source: Interestingly, infection with lab-generated Amphotericin-B-unresponsive LD promastigotes (LD-SAmp-B-R) without primary unresponsiveness toward antimony did not result in any significant lipid droplets accumulation around LD-R amastigotes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) and neither showed any significant alteration in EC50 between low (0.09 μM) and high lipid medium (0.11 μM) (Figure 8Ciii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and Figure 8Ciii.

claims.claim: Treatment with Aspirin alone did not significantly reduce the amastigote load in LD-R-infected-KCs.
claims.source: Interestingly, while treatment with Aspirin alone did not significantly reduce the amastigote load in LD-R-infected-KCs, combining Aspirin with previously determined low dose of Amp-B (0.1 μM), completely restored Amp-B responsiveness against intracellular LD-R amastigotes (Figure 8E, F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 8E, F.

claims.claim: Combining Aspirin with low dose of Amp-B (0.1 μM) completely restored Amp-B responsiveness against intracellular LD-R amastigotes.
claims.source: Interestingly, while treatment with Aspirin alone did not significantly reduce the amastigote load in LD-R-infected-KCs, combining Aspirin with previously determined low dose of Amp-B (0.1 μM), completely restored Amp-B responsiveness against intracellular LD-R amastigotes (Figure 8E, F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 8E, F.

claims.claim: VL patients who relapsed after Amp-B treatment had significantly lower serum LDL and cholesterol levels compared to Amp-B treatment responders.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with findings from human VL patients from the endemic region of Bihar, India, where those who relapsed after Amp-B treatment had significantly lower serum LDL and cholesterol levels compared to Amp-B treatment responders (Figure 8G and Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by clinical data shown in Figure 8G and Table 2.

claims.claim: LD amastigote load in splenic aspirates of VL patients exhibits an inverse correlation with serum cholesterol level.
claims.source: Previously, LD amastigote load in splenic aspirates of VL patients have been shown to exhibit an inverse correlation with serum cholesterol level (Ghosh et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Infection with antimony-unresponsive-LD (LD-R) has been previously reported to exhibit higher amastigote load in spleen and liver of infected host compared to LD-S-infection.
claims.source: Since infection with antimony-unresponsive-LD (LD-R) has been previously reported to exhibit higher amastigote load in spleen and liver of infected host, as compared to infection with their responsive counterparts (LD-S) (Vanaerschot et al., 2011; Haldar et al., 2010), we wanted to investigate possible extent of dyslipidaemia in response to LD-R and LD-S-infection and how it might affect disease pathology.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Liver serves as a primary site for lipid synthesis and liver-resident MΦs (KCs) are one of the primary sites harboring LD amastigotes.
claims.source: Liver serves as a primary site for lipid synthesis and liver-resident MΦs (KCs) are one of the primary sites harboring LD amastigotes (Beattie et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: At 72 hr post-infection, a notable number of infected KC began detaching from the wells with extracellular amastigotes probably egressing out from the infected KCs.
claims.source: Moreover, it was also noticed that at 72 hr p.i. a notable number of infected KC began detaching from the wells with extracellular amastigotes probably egressing out from the infected KCs (Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is an observation stated in the results and supported by Video 2.

claims.claim: Higher parasite load is a conserved LD-R phenotype which does not depend on initial infectivity or MΦ origin.
claims.source: Moreover, KCs infected with LD-S or LD-R amastigotes isolated from 28 days infected mouse spleens, also resulted in significantly higher parasite load for LD-R (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), clearly indicating that higher parasite load is a conserved LD-R phenotype which does not depends on initial infectivity or MΦ origin.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: 3D image reconstruction for LD-R-PV at 24 hr post-infection presented it as a larger fused structure compared to smaller individual segmented appearance of LD-S-PV.
claims.source: Interestingly, 3D image reconstruction for LD-R-PV at 24 hr p.i., presented it as a larger fused structure as compared to smaller individual segmented appearance of LD-S-PV (Figure 1Diii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1Diii.

claims.claim: LD infection in hypercholesteremic Apoe−/− mice triggers a heightened inflammatory response at approximately 6 weeks' post-infection compared to wild-type BL/6 mice.
claims.source: Previous report has suggested that LD infection in hypercholesteremic Apoe−/− mice triggers a heightened inflammatory response at approximately 6 weeks' post-infection compared to wild-type BL/6 mice, leading to more efficient parasite clearance. This is owing to unique membrane composition of Apoe−/− which rectifies leishmania-mediated defective antigen presentation at a later stage of LD infection (Ghosh et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: LD infection is well established in mice within 6–11 days post-infection in murine models.
claims.source: Additionally, previous studies have also indicated that LD infection is well established in mice within 6–11 days post-infection in murine models (Carter et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: L. mexicana can acquire host membrane cholesterol during its initial entry into host MΦs.
claims.source: Leishmania amastigotes are lipid auxotrophs (Goad et al., 1984; Bouazizi-Ben Messaoud et al., 2017), and it has been previously reported that L. mexicana can acquire host membrane cholesterol during its initial entry into host MΦs (Semini et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claims.claim: LDL serves as the primary source of cellular lipids which helps to maintain lipid homeostasis.
claims.source: LDL serves as the primary source of cellular lipids which helps to maintain lipid homeostasis, and gets readily metabolized to produce bioavailable cholesterol (Vance, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: LDL-influx is mediated by replicating LD amastigotes.
claims.source: Fluorescence plate reader-based quantification further supported this observation showing significantly higher LDL accumulation in LD-R-infected-KCs over time, which was not observed by performing infection with killed parasites (Figure 3Aii), indicating that, LDL-influx is mediated by replicating LD amastigotes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 3Aii.

claims.claim: De novo cholesterol synthesis could serve as a lipid source for intracellular LD amastigotes.
claims.source: Besides LDL endocytosis, de novo cholesterol synthesis could also serve as a lipid source for intracellular LD amastigotes (Boodhoo et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: SREBP2 regulates NPC-1 expression.
claims.source: Notably, SREBP2 regulates NPC-1 expression (Garver et al., 2008) and has been shown to get activated in response to LD-S-infection (Prakash and Rai, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Several intracellular pathogens like Mycobacterium, Toxoplasma, HCV have been reported to transfer stored triacylglycerols and sterol esters from lipid droplets to support their proliferation.
claims.source: Several intracellular pathogens like Mycobacterium, Toxoplasma, HCV have been reported to transfer stored triacylglycerols and sterol esters from lipid droplets to support their proliferation (Sonda and Hehl, 2006; Kim and Shin, 2023; Awadh, 2023).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Drug responsiveness in leishmaniasis has mostly been studied through in vitro selection of drug-resistant promastigotes, with limited focus on the drug susceptibility profiles of circulating clinical strains.
claims.source: So far, drug responsiveness in leishmaniasis has mostly been studied through in vitro selection of drug-resistant promastigotes, with limited focus on the drug susceptibility profiles of circulating clinical strains of Leishmania (Douanne et al., 2022; Légaré et al., 2001; Gourbal et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Drug responsiveness and treatment failure in VL are multifactorial, influenced by the host's immune-metabolic status.
claims.source: However, growing evidences indicate that drug responsiveness and treatment failure in VL are multifactorial, influenced by the host's immune-metabolic status (Mukherjee et al., 2013; Ghosh et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Emergence of drug unresponsiveness among intracellular pathogens has been linked with their ability to modulate host lipid metabolism.
claims.source: Importantly, recent reports have also linked emergence of drug unresponsiveness among intracellular pathogens with their ability to modulate host lipid metabolism (Sen et al., 2011; Toledo and Benach, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Increased lipid accumulation can hinder drug penetration by trapping lipophilic drugs, fostering resistance.
claims.source: For instance, increased lipid accumulation can hinder drug penetration by trapping lipophilic drugs, fostering resistance (Chang et al., 2015; Cao, 2019; Day et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: VL treatment in recent years have seen a rise in treatment failure against Amphotericin-B (Amp-B).
claims.source: VL treatment in recent years have seen a rise in treatment failure against Amphotericin-B (Amp-B), a second-line lipophilic drug (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2011), making it critical to investigate these failures in the context of lipid utilization during LD infection.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Accumulation of ox-LDL causes inflammatory response.
claims.source: Notably, accumulation of ox-LDL, and not its neutral form has been reported to cause inflammatory response (Ho et al., 2019; Govaere et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claims.claim: MSR-1 is a scavenger receptor of oxidized-LDL (ox-LDL).
claims.source: We also observed a suppressed expression of MSR-1, a scavenger receptor of oxidized-LDL (ox-LDL) (Sheng et al., 2022), in LD-R infected murine liver, suggesting LD-R-infection limits the uptake of ox-LDL, reducing inflammatory responses.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Aspirin is a lipid droplet formation blocker.
claims.source: Previously, Aspirin (Asp), a lipid droplet blocker has been reported to block lipid droplet formation in T.cruzi and LD-infected-MΦs (Banerjee et al., 2022; D'Avila et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claims.claim: MΦs primarily uptake LDL via the LDL receptor (LDLr).
claims.source: Considering that MΦs primarily uptake LDL via the LDL receptor (LDLr) (Goldstein et al., 1985), we checked its status in response to LD-S and LD-R-infection.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: MΦs can acquire LDL through receptor-independent fluid-phase endocytosis.
claims.source: Apart from LDLr, MΦs can also acquire LDL through receptor-independent fluid-phase endocytosis (Lucero et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Cofilin is an actin modulating protein which serves as a marker for fluid-phase endocytosis.
claims.source: To confirm this possibility, we checked the status of Cofilin, an actin modulating protein, which serves as a marker for fluid-phase endocytosis.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results.

claims.claim: Latrunculin-A specifically inhibits fluid-phase endocytosis by inducing actin depolymerization.
claims.source: Finally, we infected the KCs with GFP expressing LD-R for 4 hr, washed and allowed the infection to proceed in presence of fluorescent red-LDL and Latrunculin-A (5 µM), a compound which specifically inhibits fluid-phase endocytosis by inducing actin depolymerization (Lucero et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Cytochalasin-D alters cellular F-actin organization but does not affect fluid-phase endocytosis.
claims.source: In contrast, treatment with Cytochalasin-D, which alters cellular F-actin organization but does not affect fluid-phase endocytosis (Lucero et al., 2020), had no effect on the intracellular proliferation of LD-R irrespective of Cytochalasin-D concentrations (2.5 and 5 µg/ml, respectively) (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: LDL-vesicles fuse with lysosomes upon entry into MΦs, leading to subsequent transfer of LDL-derived cholesterol into the endoplasmic reticulum and cytoplasm.
claims.source: Typically, LDL-vesicles fuses with lysosomes upon entry into MΦs, leading to subsequent transfer of LDL-derived cholesterol into the endoplasmic reticulum and cytoplasm (Urano et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: LD-PV are modified phagolysosomes.
claims.source: LD-PV are modified phagolysosomes (Pessoa et al., 2019; Verma et al., 2017), and we observed an increased convergence of LDL-vesicles with LAMP-1-positive LD-R-PV even at 4 hr p.i., while such convergence was not noticed in LD-S-infected-KC (Figure 5Ai, ii).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Metabolized cholesterol is released back into cytosol from LDL-vesicles by two transmembrane proteins namely NPC-1 and NPC-2.
claims.source: Once LDL is broken down to cholesterol by lysosomal acid hydrolases, metabolized cholesterol is released back into cytosol from LDL-vesicles by two transmembrane proteins namely NPC-1 and NPC-2 (Urano et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claims.claim: SREBP2 acts as the master regulator of cholesterol biosynthesis.
claims.source: Furthermore, as SREBP2 acts as the master regulator of cholesterol biosynthesis, its downregulation and inhibition of nuclear translocation further impacted expression of the downstream cholesterol biosynthetic enzyme HMGCR (Figure 6D) specifically in LD-R-infected-KCs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: High organ parasite load linked with LD-R-infection does not rely only on initial infectivity.
claims.source: Our observations pointed out that high organ parasite load linked with LD-R-infection does not rely only on initial infectivity as commonly believed to date (Vanaerschot et al., 2011), rather is indicative of a selective higher intracellular proliferation in host.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation and experimental data.

claims.claim: LD-R-infection can regulate host proteins expression through post transcriptional and post translational modifications.
claims.source: It is possible and has been earlier reported that LD infection can regulate host proteins expression through post transcriptional and post translational modifications (Geraci et al., 2015; Tiwari et al., 2017; Moradimotlagh et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Natural clinical LD-R-isolates have developed an inherent adaptability to gradually develop cross-resistance toward Amp-B as an additional consequence of their ability to accumulate increased host-derived lipids.
claims.source: Our results thus suggest that natural clinical LD-R-isolates have developed an inherent adaptability to gradually develop cross-resistance toward Amp-B, probably as an additional consequence of their ability to accumulate increased host-derived lipids as a rapidly proliferating intracellular amastigote (represented graphically in Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data represented in Figure 9.

claims.claim: LD-R might be more adept at acquiring and metabolizing host-derived nutrients within their parasitophorous vacuole (PV), facilitating their heightened intracellular proliferation.
claims.source: This implies LD-R might be more adept at acquiring and metabolizing host-derived nutrients within their parasitophorous vacuole (PV), facilitating their heightened intracellular proliferation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of higher replicative potential of LD-R.

claims.claim: Replicating Leishmania amastigotes might co-opt host-derived lipids to facilitate their intracellular proliferation and membrane synthesis.
claims.source: all these clearly suggest replicating Leishmania amastigotes might co-opt host-derived lipids to facilitate their intracellular proliferation and membrane synthesis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple observations about Leishmania's cholesterol requirements.

claims.claim: LD-R-infection limits the uptake of ox-LDL, reducing inflammatory responses.
claims.source: We also observed a suppressed expression of MSR-1, a scavenger receptor of oxidized-LDL (ox-LDL) (Sheng et al., 2022), in LD-R infected murine liver, suggesting LD-R-infection limits the uptake of ox-LDL, reducing inflammatory responses.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of suppressed MSR-1 expression and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Lipid droplet accumulation around LD-R amastigotes contributes to Amp-B unresponsiveness by explaining recent reports of Amp-B cross-resistance in clinical LD-R-isolates from India.
claims.source: Furthermore, our findings indicate that lipid droplet accumulation around LD-R amastigotes contributes to Amp-B unresponsiveness, explaining recent reports of Amp-B cross-resistance in clinical LD-R-isolates from India (Purkait et al., 2012; Srivastava, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by citations and experimental data.

claims.claim: Higher availability of extracellular lipids might help in increased proliferation of LD-R amastigotes.
claims.source: This observation possibly indicates a higher initial infection propensity in Apoe−/− mice, which might get resolved later on due to increasing T-cell activity. Our observation also showed that splenic parasite load for LD-R is significantly higher in Apoe−/− than BL/6 (Figure 2Cii, iii) again confirming that higher availability of extracellular lipids might help in increased proliferation of LD-R amastigotes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2Cii, iii.

claims.claim: LD-R amastigotes should require significantly higher amount of host lipids to support their aggressive division.
claims.source: Thus, to support their aggressive division, LD-R amastigotes should require significantly higher amount of host lipids, which in turn will allow excess supply of cholesterol for increased PV and daughter membrane biogenesis as compared to LD-S amastigotes.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the observation of aggressive division of LD-R.

claims.claim: LD-R-induced LDL-endocytosis relies on fluid-phase endocytosis, involving significant actin cytoskeleton reorientation in LD-R-infected-MΦs.
claims.source: Interestingly, this LD-R-induced LDL-endocytosis is independent of the host's LDL receptor and relies on fluid-phase endocytosis, involving significant actin cytoskeleton reorientation in LD-R-infected-MΦs (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: LD-R-infection has been reported to induce high levels of IL-10, which is linked with enhanced fluid-phase endocytosis.
claims.source: It is worth mentioning that LD-R-infection has been reported to induce high levels of IL-10 (Mukherjee et al., 2013), which is linked with enhanced fluid-phase endocytosis (Lucero et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Higher fusion of lysosomal vesicles with LD-R-PV explains the significant Filipin-cholesterol staining around LD-R amastigotes.
claims.source: Lysosomal acid hydrolases metabolize LDL into bioavailable cholesterol, and higher fusion of lysosomal vesicles with LD-R-PV explains the significant Filipin-cholesterol staining around LD-R amastigotes (Figure 5).

claims.claim: Increased LDL-vesicle fusion probably indicates toward a rapid maturation of LD-R-PV.
claims.source: These findings not only confirm that endocytosed-LDL can be better utilized by LD-R amastigotes but probably also indicates toward a rapid maturation of LD-R-PV due to increased LDL-vesicle fusion (Sood et al., 2024; Pessoa et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on experimental findings and supported by citations.

claims.claim: LD-R amastigote might be promoting an increased lysosomal biogenesis through post transcriptional and post translational modifications to increase supply of bioavailable cholesterol.
claims.source: It is tempting to speculate that LD-R amastigote might be promoting an increased lysosomal biogenesis through any such mechanism to increase supply of bioavailable cholesterol through action of lysosomal acid hydrolases on LDL.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on observations and previous reports.

claims.claim: Suppressed expression of NPC-1 correlates with higher cholesterol availability for aggressive LD-R proliferation.
claims.source: NPC-1 is crucial for mobilizing vesicular cholesterol to the cytoplasm and plasma membrane (Urano et al., 2008), and its suppressed expression correlates with higher cholesterol availability for aggressive LD-R proliferation (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 6 and supported by citation.

claims.claim: LD-R-infected macrophages preferentially rely on endocytosed-LDL-derived cholesterol rather than de novo synthesized cholesterol to support their metabolic needs.
claims.source: Downregulation of HMGCS which catalyzes the condensation of acetyl-CoA with acetoacetyl-CoA to form 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA), which serves as an intermediate in both cholesterol biosynthesis and ketogenesis further supports our observation that LD-R-infected PECs preferentially rely on endocytosed-LDL-derived cholesterol rather than de novo synthesized cholesterol to support their metabolic needs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from RNAseq data showing downregulation of hmgcs.

claims.claim: Close proximity of lipid droplets with LD-R amastigotes makes it tempting to speculate existence of lipid droplets contact sites.
claims.source: Close proximity lipid droplets with LD-R amastigotes makes it tempting to speculate existence of lipid droplets contact sites (Sood et al., 2024), or possible copy number variations in these lipid metabolizing genes (Downing et al., 2011), providing survival advantages to LD-R.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on observations and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Eliminating lipid droplets around LD-R amastigotes might be a weapon of choice to combat treatment failure against Amp-B.
claims.source: Fact that LD-R amastigotes regained their responsiveness toward Amp-B in low lipid medium or in presence of Aspirin (Banerjee et al., 2022), further confirms that eliminating lipid droplets around LD-R amastigotes might be a weapon of choice to combat treatment failure against Amp-B (Purkait et al., 2012; Srivastava, 2011; Patole et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and supported by citations.

results.result: LD-R infection causes more severe dyslipidemia than LD-S infection, with significantly lower serum LDL, HDL, and cholesterol levels in LD-R-infected mice compared to LD-S-infected mice. This severe dyslipidemia correlates with higher organ parasite burden in LD-R infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C21 and C58 provide direct experimental evidence showing significantly lower serum lipid levels in LD-R-infected mice (Figure 1A) and an inverse correlation between parasite load and cholesterol levels. Claims C1, C2, C3, C20, and C59 provide supporting context from prior literature establishing the relationship between VL, hypolipidemia, and LD's cholesterol auxotrophy.

results.result: LD-R exhibits significantly higher intracellular proliferation than LD-S in Kupffer cells, with exponential replication between 4-24 hours post-infection. This higher parasite load is a conserved LD-R phenotype independent of initial infectivity or macrophage origin.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 provide direct experimental evidence from Figure 1 showing no difference in initial attachment but significantly higher amastigote numbers at 24 hr for LD-R. Claims C62-C63 confirm this is a conserved phenotype with additional structural observations. The temporal dynamics and independence from initial infectivity are well-documented.

results.result: LD-R proliferation is highly dependent on extracellular lipid availability. Lipid deprivation severely compromises LD-R but not LD-S proliferation, while hyperlipidemic conditions (ApoE-/- mice) significantly increase LD-R but not LD-S amastigote load.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 provide complementary experimental evidence from Figure 2 using both lipid deprivation and hyperlipidemic mouse models. The differential effects on LD-R versus LD-S are consistently demonstrated across multiple experimental conditions, strongly supporting LD-R's heightened lipid dependency.

results.result: Both LD-S and LD-R extract NBD-cholesterol from KC membranes during initial infection (4 hr p.i.) with comparable efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 is directly supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ai, ii showing no significant difference in membrane cholesterol extraction between LD-S and LD-R at early infection timepoints. This establishes that differential lipid acquisition occurs after initial infection.

results.result: LD-R-infected KCs accumulate significantly more LDL and cholesterol than LD-S-infected cells. Multiple analytical methods (live cell imaging, confocal microscopy, Amplex Red assay, TLC, GC-MS, and Raman spectroscopy) demonstrate higher cholesterol, fatty acids, and lipid content in LD-R-PV compared to LD-S-PV.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 provide convergent evidence from multiple independent analytical techniques (Figures 3 and supplements) all demonstrating elevated lipid accumulation in LD-R infections. Claim C68 confirms this is mediated by replicating amastigotes. The consistency across diverse methodologies strongly supports this result.

results.result: LD-R promotes LDL uptake through LDL receptor-independent fluid-phase endocytosis involving cofilin-mediated actin cytoskeleton remodeling. Latrunculin-A (fluid-phase endocytosis inhibitor) but not Cytochalasin-D blocks LDL uptake and LD-R proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 provide comprehensive evidence from Figure 4 using LDLr knockdown, cofilin expression analysis, and pharmacological inhibitors. The differential effects of Latrunculin-A versus Cytochalasin-D provide strong mechanistic support for fluid-phase endocytosis as the primary LDL uptake mechanism in LD-R infection.

results.result: LD-R enhances fusion of endocytosed LDL-vesicles with LAMP-1-positive parasitophorous vacuoles. Structured illumination microscopy shows complete convergence of LDL-vesicles with LD-R-PV at 24 hr, with enhanced cholesterol accumulation around LD-R amastigotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 provide direct imaging evidence from Figure 5 showing increased LDL-vesicle fusion with LD-R-PV at both early (4 hr) and late (24 hr) timepoints. Filipin staining confirms enhanced cholesterol accumulation. The temporal progression and specificity to LD-R infection are well-documented.

results.result: LD-R suppresses NPC-1 expression and SREBP2 nuclear translocation, inhibiting cholesterol mobilization from LDL-vesicles. siRNA-mediated NPC-1 knockdown increases LD-R but not LD-S amastigote load, confirming NPC-1's role in limiting LD-R proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 provide convergent evidence from RNAseq, western blot, confocal imaging, and functional knockdown experiments (Figure 6). The specificity of NPC-1 suppression to LD-R infection and the differential effect of NPC-1 knockdown on LD-R versus LD-S strongly support this mechanism.

results.result: LD-R infection selectively excludes oxidized-LDL uptake by suppressing MSR-1 expression, accumulating neutral lipids while limiting inflammatory responses. LD-R-infected KCs show low IFN-γ levels and reduced ox-LDL uptake compared to LD-S.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 provide comprehensive evidence from Figure 7 including cytokine measurements, ox-LDL staining, MSR-1 expression analysis, and in vivo liver immunostaining. The selective exclusion of ox-LDL while accumulating neutral lipids explains the paradoxical lack of inflammation despite high lipid accumulation.

results.result: Excess LDL influx leads to accumulation of neutral lipid droplets around LD-R amastigotes. Multiple imaging modalities (Nile red staining, expansion microscopy, TEM) confirm significantly higher lipid droplet accumulation around LD-R compared to LD-S amastigotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 provide direct visualization evidence from Figure 8 and supplements using complementary imaging techniques. The consistency across different imaging modalities (fluorescence, expansion microscopy, electron microscopy) strongly supports lipid droplet accumulation as a characteristic feature of LD-R infection.

results.result: Lipid droplet accumulation around LD-R amastigotes increases Amphotericin-B unresponsiveness. Low lipid medium or Aspirin treatment reduces lipid droplets and restores Amp-B responsiveness in LD-R. Lab-generated Amp-B-resistant strains without antimony resistance do not show this lipid-dependent phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 provide comprehensive evidence from Figure 8 showing EC50 values under different lipid conditions and with Aspirin treatment. Claim C54 provides a critical control showing this is specific to clinical LD-R isolates. The restoration of drug sensitivity by lipid droplet reduction provides strong causal evidence.

results.result: VL patients who relapsed after Amphotericin-B treatment had significantly lower serum LDL and cholesterol levels compared to cured patients, consistent with the experimental findings linking low serum lipids to increased parasite lipid scavenging and drug resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C10 and C57 provide clinical validation from human VL patients (Figure 8G, Table 2) that directly parallels the experimental findings. The consistency between clinical observations and experimental mechanisms strengthens the translational relevance of the findings.

results.result: Antimony-resistant LD isolates persist despite drug withdrawal and exhibit greater replicative potential than sensitive strains, offering selective intracellular survival advantages beyond initial metacyclogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C16 establish the clinical and biological context for the study, supported by multiple citations. These claims provide essential background establishing that LD-R represents a persistent phenotype with enhanced replicative capacity, setting up the mechanistic investigations.

results.result: Leishmania parasites are cholesterol auxotrophs requiring host membrane cholesterol for infection and accumulating cholesterol and lipid droplets within parasitophorous vacuoles during intracellular replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19 are well-established facts from prior literature (supported by multiple citations) that provide the biological rationale for investigating lipid metabolism in LD infection. Claim C93 represents a logical inference from these established facts.

results.result: Kupffer cells serve as a primary site for LD infection and lipid synthesis. LD infection dynamics show exponential replication between 4-24 hours with parasite egress beginning around 72 hours. Various contextual facts about lipid metabolism and infection timing are established.
results.evaluation: These claims provide methodological justification and contextual information supported by citations and observational data (Video 2). They establish KCs as an appropriate model system and provide temporal context for the infection studies.

results.result: De novo cholesterol synthesis could serve as an alternative lipid source for LD amastigotes. SREBP2 regulates NPC-1 expression and acts as the master regulator of cholesterol biosynthesis.
results.evaluation: These claims establish known biological relationships from prior literature (supported by citations) that provide context for understanding the experimental findings regarding SREBP2 and NPC-1 suppression in LD-R infection.

results.result: Intracellular pathogens commonly manipulate host lipid metabolism for survival, and drug resistance in VL is multifactorial, influenced by host immune-metabolic status. Lipid accumulation can hinder drug penetration, and Amphotericin-B treatment failures are increasing.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the broader scientific context from prior literature (supported by multiple citations) that motivates the study's focus on lipid metabolism and drug resistance. They provide the rationale for investigating lipid-mediated drug resistance mechanisms.

results.result: Various established facts about lipid metabolism, receptors, and cellular processes are cited: ox-LDL causes inflammation; MSR-1 is an ox-LDL receptor; Aspirin blocks lipid droplets; macrophages uptake LDL via LDLr and fluid-phase endocytosis; cofilin marks fluid-phase endocytosis; Latrunculin-A and Cytochalasin-D have distinct effects on endocytosis; LDL-vesicles fuse with lysosomes; LD-PV are modified phagolysosomes; NPC-1/2 mobilize cholesterol.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established biological knowledge from prior literature (all supported by citations) that provide the mechanistic framework for interpreting the experimental findings. They are appropriately cited and accurately represent the referenced work.

results.result: High organ parasite load in LD-R infection reflects selective higher intracellular proliferation rather than just initial infectivity. LD-R has developed inherent adaptability to accumulate host-derived lipids and develop cross-resistance to Amphotericin-B.
results.evaluation: These claims represent interpretive conclusions drawn from the collective experimental evidence. Claims C89 and C92 are supported by the proliferation data (Figures 1-2). Claims C91 and C97 represent reasonable inferences from the lipid accumulation and drug resistance data, though they involve some speculation about evolutionary adaptation.

results.result: Several mechanistic speculations are proposed: LD-R may regulate host proteins through post-transcriptional/translational modifications; LD-R infection induces IL-10 linked to fluid-phase endocytosis; increased LDL-vesicle fusion may indicate rapid PV maturation; LD-R may promote lysosomal biogenesis; LD-R-infected macrophages preferentially use LDL-derived rather than de novo cholesterol; lipid droplet contact sites may exist; eliminating lipid droplets may combat Amp-B resistance.
results.evaluation: These claims represent speculative interpretations and mechanistic hypotheses. While they are reasonable inferences from the data and prior literature, they lack direct experimental validation in this study. Claims C90, C99, C101, C102, and C105 are explicitly marked as speculation. Claims C104 and C106 are more strongly supported by the data but still represent interpretations requiring further validation.

results.result: LD-R parasites undergo logarithmic growth between 4 and 24 hours in infected cells, with significantly higher amastigote numbers at 24 hr compared to LD-S. This growth slows down after 24 hours, and the higher parasite load is a conserved LD-R phenotype independent of initial infectivity or macrophage origin.
results.evaluation: The reviewer explicitly states this is 'a puzzling observation for which they provide compelling evidence' regarding 'the capacity of LD-R parasites to undergo logarithmic growth between 4 and 24 hours in infected cells.' The reviewer notes the evidence is compelling and acknowledges the observation that 'parasite growth slows down inexplicably after 24 hours.'

results.result: LD-R infection shows increased convergence of LDL-vesicles with LAMP-1-positive parasitophorous vacuoles (PV) at 4 hr post-infection, with complete convergence confirmed by structured illumination microscopy at 24 hr. In contrast, LD-S-PV showed only partial convergence even at 24 hr.
results.evaluation: The reviewer made 'the novel observation that Lamp1 expression increases as early as 4 hours after infection with LD-R and by 12 hours after infection with both LD-S and LD-R.' This directly relates to the increased convergence of LDL-vesicles with LAMP-1-positive PV, and the reviewer treats this as a validated finding.

results.result: LD-R infection promotes fluid-phase endocytosis in host macrophages, leading to significantly higher LDL accumulation in LD-R-infected cells compared to LD-S. This LDL uptake is independent of the LDL receptor and relies on fluid-phase endocytosis involving actin cytoskeleton reorientation, as demonstrated by cofilin activation and sensitivity to Latrunculin-A but not Cytochalasin-D.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers affirm this finding. The first reviewer states the authors 'present compelling evidence that supports this hypothesis' regarding lipid scavenging. The second reviewer explicitly notes 'The authors present compelling evidence that supports their hypothesis' about the parasites' capacity to acquire and utilize lipids, which encompasses the fluid-phase endocytosis mechanism.

results.result: LD-R enhances fusion of LDL-vesicles with its phagolysosomal membrane and inhibits cholesterol mobilization by suppressing NPC-1 expression and preventing SREBP2 nuclear translocation. siRNA-mediated knockdown of NPC-1 increased LD-R amastigote load, confirming the role of NPC-1 suppression in LD-R proliferation.
results.evaluation: The reviewer notes 'Interestingly, transcription analysis did not provide evidence for increased Lamp1 transcripts, leaving open the possibility that parasite infection may exert control over host cell biology at the translational level.' This acknowledgment of post-transcriptional control mechanisms supports the authors' findings about NPC-1 suppression and SREBP2 regulation, though the reviewer notes the mechanism remains an open question.

results.result: LD-R infection selectively accumulates neutral lipids while excluding oxidized-LDL through suppressed MSR-1 expression. This leads to accumulation of neutral lipid droplets around LD-R amastigotes, confirmed by lipid droplet staining and TEM, while reducing inflammatory responses by limiting ox-LDL uptake.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer states the study 'adds to other work that has implicated pathogen-derived processes in the selective recruitment of vesicles to the pathogen-containing vacuole, based on the content of the cargo.' This directly supports the selective accumulation of neutral lipids while excluding oxidized-LDL. The second reviewer affirms the authors 'present compelling evidence' for their hypothesis about lipid utilization.

results.result: Accumulation of neutral lipid droplets around LD-R amastigotes increases their unresponsiveness toward Amphotericin-B. Low lipid medium or Aspirin treatment reduced lipid droplets and restored Amp-B responsiveness, suggesting natural clinical LD-R-isolates have developed cross-resistance to Amp-B as a consequence of their lipid accumulation.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly discusses 'The basis for the beneficial effect of aspirin to stifle parasite resistance to antimony,' indicating acceptance of the aspirin findings. Both reviewers affirm the overall hypothesis with 'compelling evidence,' which encompasses the drug resistance mechanism linked to lipid accumulation.

results.result: VL patients showing relapse with Amphotericin-B treatment exhibited significantly lower serum LDL and cholesterol levels compared to cured cases, consistent with clinical data from Bihar, India.
results.evaluation: While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, this clinical finding is part of the overall body of evidence that both reviewers describe as 'compelling.' The reviewers' general acceptance of the lipid-drug resistance hypothesis implicitly supports this clinical correlation.

results.result: Mice infected with LD-R showed significantly lower serum lipid levels compared to LD-S. LD-R proliferation was severely compromised in low lipid medium but increased in KCs from hyperlipidemic ApoE-knockout mice, confirming LD-R's dependency on external lipid availability.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer states 'The hypothesis that these authors set out to test is that these parasites have developed a new capacity to acquire and utilize lipids, especially cholesterol, which enables them to grow robustly in infected hosts. The authors present compelling evidence that supports their hypothesis.' This directly supports the lipid dependency findings.

results.result: LD-R exhibits more aggressive pathology with increased organ parasite burden compared to LD-S in both clinical and experimental infections. This high parasite load does not rely only on initial infectivity but indicates selective higher intracellular proliferation.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly states 'It is of interest to determine the properties that favor the retention of their drug resistance phenotype even in the absence of the selective pressure that the drug would otherwise exert,' acknowledging the persistent aggressive phenotype. Both reviewers accept the overall findings with 'compelling evidence.'

results.result: Background claims establishing that VL is characterized by hypolipidemia, Leishmania donovani is a cholesterol auxotroph requiring host lipids for survival, and intracellular amastigotes accumulate cholesterol and lipid droplets. These foundational claims support the hypothesis that replicating amastigotes co-opt host-derived lipids for proliferation.
results.evaluation: These are established background facts that both reviewers implicitly accept as the foundation for the study. The second reviewer states 'The hypothesis that these authors set out to test is that these parasites have developed a new capacity to acquire and utilize lipids,' acknowledging these foundational concepts.

results.result: Background claims about antimony withdrawal, persistent LD-R phenotype, and the multifactorial nature of drug responsiveness in VL, including links between drug unresponsiveness and host lipid metabolism modulation.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly acknowledges 'Although the use of antimony has been discontinued in India, the observation that Leishmania parasites resistant to antimony are in circulation has been cited as evidence that these resistant parasites are now a distinct strain.' This validates the background context.

results.result: LD-S and LD-R showed no significant difference in initial attachment to host membrane or in extracting NBD-cholesterol during initial infection (4 hr). However, 3D reconstruction showed LD-R-PV as a larger fused structure compared to LD-S-PV at 24 hr.
results.evaluation: These findings are part of the characterization of LD-R behavior that both reviewers describe as supported by 'compelling evidence.' The reviewers do not challenge these specific observations.

results.result: LD-R-infected KCs showed low IFN-γ levels even after 24 hr of co-culture with T-cells, while LD-S-infection showed significant increase at this time point.
results.evaluation: This finding relates to the inflammatory response differences between LD-R and LD-S. While not explicitly discussed, it is part of the overall body of evidence that reviewers describe as 'compelling.'

results.result: Various mechanistic and background claims about metacyclogenesis, replicative potential, lipid metabolism pathways, inflammatory responses, and technical details about cellular processes and drug mechanisms.
results.evaluation: These are supporting mechanistic details and background information that reviewers implicitly accept as part of the overall 'compelling evidence.' They are not challenged or questioned.

results.result: Various inferential and speculative claims about mechanisms, including observations about KC detachment, LDL-influx mediation, post-transcriptional regulation, lipid requirements, lysosomal biogenesis, and therapeutic implications.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer notes 'the genetic basis for the parasite's gluttony for lipids remains unresolved' and that transcription analysis 'leaving open the possibility that parasite infection may exert control over host cell biology at the translational level. How this might be achieved and what genes would be targets for such controls are open questions.' This indicates uncertainty about the underlying mechanisms, even though the phenotypic observations are accepted.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect match on clinical findings (C10, C57). Both evaluations support the correlation between lipid levels and drug resistance in human VL patients. OpenEval provides explicit validation while peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of the 'compelling evidence' for the overall hypothesis.

Strong agreement on drug resistance mechanisms (C9, C52-C56, C95). Both evaluations support the lipid-mediated drug resistance findings and aspirin's beneficial effect. OpenEval emphasizes the causal evidence from lipid droplet reduction, while peer reviewers explicitly discuss aspirin's effect on antimony resistance.

Strong agreement on NPC-1 suppression and SREBP2 regulation (C6, C7, C42-C45, C103). Both evaluations support these findings. Peer reviewers note the mechanism remains an open question regarding translational control, while OpenEval emphasizes the convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches.

Strong agreement on lipid dependency (C25-C27, C96). Both evaluations support the differential effects on LD-R versus LD-S under various lipid conditions. Peer reviewers describe the evidence as 'compelling' for the hypothesis that parasites have developed enhanced capacity to acquire and utilize lipids.

Strong agreement on enhanced replication phenotype (C23, C24, C62). Both evaluations support the logarithmic growth between 4-24 hours. Peer reviewers describe this as 'a puzzling observation for which they provide compelling evidence' and note the unexplained slowdown after 24 hours.

Strong agreement on fluid-phase endocytosis mechanism (C4, C34-C38, C98). Both evaluations support the LDL uptake mechanism. Peer reviewers affirm the authors 'present compelling evidence that supports their hypothesis' about lipid acquisition capacity.

Agreement on LDL-vesicle fusion with PV (C39, C40). OpenEval emphasizes temporal progression at 4hr and 24hr timepoints. Peer reviewers note the 'novel observation' of increased Lamp1 expression as early as 4 hours with LD-R, treating this as validated.

Agreement on elevated lipid accumulation (C29-C33). OpenEval emphasizes convergent evidence from multiple analytical techniques. Peer reviewers support this as part of the 'compelling evidence' for the lipid scavenging hypothesis, though they focus more on the overall mechanism than specific techniques.

Agreement on selective lipid accumulation (C5, C47-C49, C94). Both evaluations support the selective recruitment of neutral lipids while excluding oxidized-LDL. Peer reviewers note this 'adds to other work that has implicated pathogen-derived processes in the selective recruitment of vesicles.'

Agreement on lipid droplet accumulation (C8, C50, C51). OpenEval emphasizes consistency across multiple imaging modalities. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall 'compelling evidence' for lipid utilization mechanisms.

Agreement on background context regarding drug resistance (C72-C76). Both evaluations support this established literature. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge that 'resistant parasites are now a distinct strain' and validate the background context.

Agreement on foundational concepts (C1, C2, C17-C20, C58, C93). OpenEval categorizes these as supporting context from prior literature. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these as the foundation for the study's hypothesis about lipid acquisition capacity.

Agreement on clinical and biological context (C12, C13). Both evaluations support the background establishing LD-R as a persistent phenotype. Peer reviewers acknowledge the circulation of resistant parasites as evidence of a distinct strain.

Agreement on biological rationale (C17-C19, C93). OpenEval treats these as well-established facts providing rationale for investigating lipid metabolism. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these foundational concepts when acknowledging the study's hypothesis.

Agreement on mechanistic framework (C77-C87). Both evaluations support these established biological concepts from prior literature. OpenEval emphasizes they provide the mechanistic framework for interpretation. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these as part of the overall evidence base.

Agreement on differential lipid acquisition timing (C28). OpenEval supports this with Figure 3 data showing no difference at early timepoints. Peer reviewers do not explicitly challenge this observation, accepting it as part of the 'compelling evidence.'

Agreement on methodological justification (C60, C61, C64-C67). OpenEval supports these as establishing KCs as an appropriate model system. Peer reviewers implicitly accept the methodological choices as part of the overall study design.

Agreement on biological relationships (C69, C70, C88). OpenEval treats these as known relationships from prior literature. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these as part of the mechanistic framework, though they note some mechanisms remain open questions.

Agreement on persistent aggressive phenotype (C89). Both evaluations support this interpretive conclusion. Peer reviewers explicitly state 'It is of interest to determine the properties that favor the retention of their drug resistance phenotype,' acknowledging the persistent nature.
